body.text: Rohingya in Australia welcome UN court's ruling Myanmar committed genocide
In short:
The International Court of Justice on Thursday delivered its judgement that Myanmar had committed genocide against the country's Rohingya Muslim minority group.
Rohingya living in Australia have welcomed the development saying it represents recognition for the suffering endured and hope for the younger generation.
What's next?
But they say the ruling must be backed up by action from the international community including Australia.
There were celebrations in suburban Brisbane last night as the International Court of Justice delivered its judgement that Myanmar had committed genocide against the country's Rohingya people.
Robi Alam, president of the Rohingya United Youth Network, said members had gathered at the group's Logan youth centre to watch the proceedings.
He said they were in touch with relatives and friends back in the Cox's Bazar refugee camp in Bangladesh where "thousands and thousands" were gathered to watch the hearing.
"A lot of them were in tears,"
"We also had a couple of brothers that were crying [here] last night, because this means that … it feels like the world will finally listen."

The United Nations' court found that a campaign mounted by Myanmar's security forces that killed thousands and perpetrated widespread sexual violence against the long-persecuted Rohingya Muslim minority population in 2017 amounted to genocide.
It was the first time the court held a state responsible for committing genocide.
The government said the campaign in Myanmar's western Rakhine State was launched in response to a series of guerilla-style attacks by a Rohingya militant group.
The army conducted massive "clearance operations" that targeted Rohingya villages. Survivors described massacres, rape, arson and looting.
According to the court, about 10,000 Rohingya people were killed and more than 700,000 forced to flee to Bangladesh.
The military insisted the Rohingya had burned their own homes and the government said there was no direct evidence of genocidal intent.
Mr Alam was born in a camp in Bangladesh and came as a refugee to Australia with his family when he was 10.
He said that he grew up like many Rohingya young people hearing stories of persecution, loss and displacement.
"For our parents and grandparents, this judgement represents recognition of the suffering they endured," he said.
"For my generation, it represents hope that our children may one day inherit a future different from the one we were born into."
Sydney Rohingya youth leader, Asma Nayim Ullah, who fled Myanmar with her family and arrived as a refugee in Australia when she was 10, said that justice was long-awaited.

"This is recognition that what we were saying wasn't false claims, or being accused that we were burning down our own homes by the Myanmar government. Finally this is being recognised as a genocide," said Ms Nayim Ullah, who is co-founder of the Australian Rohingya Women's Development Organisation (ARWDO).
"I'm relieved that we have finally reached this milestone together as it has been a long journey."
Whether that recognition translates into lasting change is another question.
Four years after the military operation targeting the Rohingya, a military coup sparked a civil war that is still wracking the country.
One of Ms Nayim Ullah's family members remained in Myanmar until a recent wave of attacks by the Myanmar military drove her to flee.
"Obviously, we don't want to live in camps, but for us to go back it needs to be safe," she said.
"I welcome the opportunities this verdict presents to secure justice and hold Myanmar accountable.
"The priority now is determining our next steps and what actions can we take to support Rohingya communities who remain displaced without safety and dignity."
What happens now?

The top UN court said Myanmar must allow the "safe and dignified return to their place of residence and the reunification of families for the Rohingya displaced as a result of Myanmar's wrongful acts".
It also said Myanmar had an obligation to compensate the Rohingya for the violations it had committed, to be determined at a later date.
These orders are legally binding, but the court has no enforcement powers of its own.
Sydney-based immigration lawyer Ko Ko Aung said the decision was symbolic, and what it would mean for the many Rohingya refugees still living in camps was unclear.
He said the facts in the case were obvious but the bar to prove genocide was high.
"I believe it is [thanks to] the real hard work of everybody involved in documenting and all the evidence that has been produced for so many years," he said.
Mr Alam said that while the judgement was welcome, it would not restore citizenship, return stolen homes or bring displaced families back together.

"The international community, including Australia, must now translate this judgement into meaningful action through diplomatic pressure, accountability, humanitarian assistance and support for a safe, voluntary and dignified return to Myanmar when conditions allow," he said.
A statement from Foreign Minister Penny Wong said Australia had "consistently condemned the Myanmar military's grave human rights abuses and called for those responsible to face justice".

Senator Wong said Australia had committed more than $1.26 billion in humanitarian assistance to people affected by the crisis in Myanmar and Bangladesh, including Rohingya refugees and their host communities, since 2017.
"We call on Myanmar to comply fully with the Court's judgement and its obligations under international law," she said.
